name: Nora Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say is confidential, so you can give me your public answer and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's all right. I'm not one for surveys, but the vicar's wife said you were decent. Ask what you like, and I'll tell you straight.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Whitlock family on Glebe House Farm, 280 hectares of sheep, beef cattle, wheat and oats. I came at twenty and I've been there twenty-three years, so I'm stock manager in all but name. I'm out at six with the dogs, Bess and Fly, checking the ewes, then it's feeding, dosing, moving stock, and harvest when it's harvest. What wears me out is the forms the government sends, but young Mark Whitlock does those, thank goodness.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Daniel drives a milk tanker, collecting from the dairies all round the county. We've Ruth, who's thirteen, and Isaac, who's nine, and a mortgage on our house in Ashby. We've always been savers, so there's well over a year put by. Sundays we're at the chapel, and I do the flowers once a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and I'd say it at the chapel and in the farm shop. People got very excited about machines that talk. I don't go online, so that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, and I'm glad. Mark might use something on the computer for the forms, but the ewes still need lambing and the dogs still need working. A computer can fill in Mark Whitlock's (her employer's) forms, but a computer can't whistle my dog Bess round a field of ewes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do. Same farm, same dogs, same hours. We'd keep saving like we always have and pay down the house a bit faster if we could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased. I don't like fuss, and this is no fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already worrying you, about work or money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Old Mr Whitlock is seventy-eight and Mark will take over, but Mark's a good lad and he knows what I do. My knees aren't what they were, but I've years left in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever tried any of these AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. Ruth showed me one on her phone and asked it about sheep, and half of what it said was wrong. That told me all I needed to know.

say: I'd say **I told you so** at the chapel and the farm shop.
think: It means **nothing for me**, and I'm glad.
Mark Whitlock might use a computer for **forms**, but the ewes still need lambing.
do: Carry on with the same **farm, dogs and hours**.
Keep **saving** and pay the house down faster if we can.
feel: Calm and **pleased**, because there's no fuss.
S0.quote: A computer can fill in Mark Whitlock's (her employer's) forms, but a computer can't whistle my dog Bess round a field of ewes.
fieldNote: Nora has **twenty-three years** on Glebe House Farm and strong loyalty to the Whitlocks.
She dismissed AI after **Ruth's phone** gave wrong answers about sheep.
Her security rests on savings and **trust in Mark**, the next owner.

steps.text: Keep the same stock job, dogs and hours at Glebe House
Overpay the Ashby house mortgage when there's spare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's for offices and young people, and farms will go on being farms. At chapel I'd say we should look after the people who lose their jobs, the way communities always have. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think my job is fine, but Daniel's isn't so sure. The dairy company already plans his routes on a computer, and if a program does more of that, they'll want fewer drivers working longer. My husband Daniel has driven the same milk route for fifteen years, and a computer would tell him how to do it in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job just as I do. We'd put a bit more aside each month in case Daniel's hours get cut. I wouldn't touch any AI, and if Mark asked me to, I'd ask him to show me first and then probably say no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be fine at work, but I'd be watching Daniel's face when he came in at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Mark asked you to use a new herd system, what would you actually say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll keep my notebook, Mark, and you can put whatever you like in the computer. He'd let me, because he knows I'm right more than the machine is. If he insisted, I'd learn the bare minimum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on if things got harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, then the chapel. Daniel's brother has a building firm and would take him on if it came to it. That's how it should be, people looking after their own, not waiting for the government.

say: I'd say AI is for **offices and young people**, and farms stay farms.
I'd say at chapel that **communities** should look after those who lose jobs.
think: My job is fine, but **Daniel's tanker job** is less sure.
The dairy company would want **fewer drivers** working longer routes.
do: Keep doing the **stock job** just as I do.
Put **more aside** each month in case Daniel's hours are cut.
Refuse AI and learn **the bare minimum** only if Mark insists.
feel: Uneasy, **watching Daniel's face** when he comes in at night.
S1.quote: My husband Daniel has driven the same milk route for fifteen years, and a computer would tell him how to do it in a week.
fieldNote: Her own hands-on job looks safe; the risk is **Daniel's route planning**.
Her safety net is **family and chapel**, not government.
Resistance is firm but **polite**: notebook stays, computer is Mark's.

steps.text: Keep doing the stock work with the dogs and notebook
Put more aside each month in case Daniel's hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and it's happening too fast, and somebody in charge should have stopped it. At chapel I'd say we must look after each other. I'd vote for whoever said they'd protect working families and farms, though I don't trust most of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think we're in real trouble. Daniel's tanker could drive itself by 2031, and a robot that can lamb ewes and work dogs would take my job the same year. Twenty-three years on Glebe House Farm, and I'd lose my job to a machine in the same year my husband loses his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd stop spending on anything but the house and the children. No new car, no holiday, nothing. We'd put every spare penny into paying the mortgage off before 2031, and I'd talk to Mark straight about what he plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd pray about it, and I'd still lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots about 3 years later. What do those three years mean for you and Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we'd know it's coming and still have work while we get ready. The office side goes first, Mark's forms, and the dairy's route planning. Then in 2031 our hands go. Three years to clear the house, that's what I'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on family. Does that still hold here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's brother's building firm would be in the same boat if robots can build. So I don't know. We'd have the savings and the chapel, but I don't want charity, I want work.

say: I'd say it's **wrong and too fast**, and someone should have stopped it.
I'd vote for whoever **protects working families**, though I don't trust most.
think: I'd lose my job and Daniel his **in the same year**.
Family help may fail too if **robots can build**.
do: Stop **all spending** except the house and children: no car, no holiday.
Pour spare money into **clearing the mortgage** before 2031.
Ask Mark **straight** what he plans for the farm.
S2.quote: Twenty-three years on Glebe House Farm, and I'd lose my job to a machine in the same year my husband loses his.
fieldNote: She expects **both household incomes** to go in 2031.
Her pride shows: **no charity**, she wants work.
She blames **those in charge** for not stopping it.

steps.text: Cancel the car purchase and the family holiday
Put every spare pound into clearing the mortgage by 2031
Vote for candidates who promise to protect family farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for the government to make sure working people aren't thrown out. I'd say it at the farm shop and to our councillor. I'd say families should stick together through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the job, just around 2034. By then I'd be fifty-one with the house nearly paid. That's frightening, but we'd have a few years to work out what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving, and we'd aim to have the house paid off by 2033. I'd talk to Daniel about whether his brother's firm, or something else local, could take him before 2034. I'd make sure Ruth and Isaac think about trades where you have to be there in person, nursing, building, that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not like the fast one. More like knowing a hard winter's coming and getting the hay in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on. What changes for you in 2031, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very little for me, I think, because Mark does the planning and the paperwork. He'd ask the computer when to sell the lambs instead of asking his dad. Then in 2034 it reaches me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth wants to work with animals, like me. I'd tell my daughter Ruth to become a nurse, because sick people will always want a real woman holding their hand.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for government to protect working people.
I'd tell our councillor that **families should stick together** through it.
think: I'd still **lose the job**, just around 2034 at fifty-one.
There'd be **a few years** to work out what comes next.
do: Keep working and saving to **pay off the house** by 2033.
Help Daniel find **local work** with his brother's firm before 2034.
Steer Ruth and Isaac towards **in-person trades** like nursing and building.
feel: Worried, like **getting the hay in** before a hard winter.
S3.quote: I'd tell my daughter Ruth to become a nurse, because sick people will always want a real woman holding their hand.
fieldNote: Five years gives her **time to prepare**, which eases the fear somewhat.
She still expects to **lose her job** but feels some control.
Her career advice is **traditional and practical**: nursing and building.

steps.text: Pay off the Ashby house by 2033
Steer Ruth towards nursing and Isaac towards a building trade
Ask Daniel's brother about taking Daniel on before 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly and there's no excuse for anyone not ready. I'd say young people should learn real skills, not just screens. At chapel I'd say look after the old ones who can't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think we'd manage. By 2039 I'm fifty-six, the house is paid, and we'd have savings. I'd want a small place of our own by then, a few acres, so I'm never at a machine's mercy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Glebe House while it lasts. Around 2035, Daniel and I would buy ten or twelve acres near Ashby with our savings, and I'd keep a small flock and sell lamb to people who want it reared the old way. That's my plan, and I'd stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. But I'd feel I had my own ground under my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a few acres of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because land is the only thing nobody can take off you if you've paid for it. If I own ten acres and fifty ewes, no robot and no boss can ever tell me I'm not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone buy lamb reared the old way when robots can do it cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. People round here like to know who reared their meat. It won't make us rich, but with the house paid it'll keep us busy and paid.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** for anyone not to be ready in ten years.
I'd urge young people to learn **real skills**, not just screens.
think: We'd **manage**: by 2039 I'm fifty-six with the house paid.
I'd want **a few acres** of our own so I'm never at a machine's mercy.
do: Keep working at **Glebe House** while it lasts.
Buy **ten or twelve acres** near Ashby with savings around 2035.
Keep a **small flock** and sell lamb reared the old way.
feel: A little uneasy, but with **her own ground** under her feet.
S4.quote: If I own ten acres and fifty ewes, no robot and no boss can ever tell me I'm not needed.
fieldNote: A decade lets her build a **traditional safety net**: owned land.
Independence from bosses and machines is **her core value**.
She is realistic that the flock **won't make them rich**.

steps.text: Buy ten or twelve acres near Ashby around 2035
Rear a small flock and sell lamb to local buyers
Keep working at Glebe House Farm until the robots come

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Daniel and I would both lose our work in the same year with the house not paid. What would help is the government making firms keep people on longer, so it's not all at once. And help for families buying a bit of land, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the dogs. Bess and Fly have worked those hills with me for years. Nobody asks what happens to a working sheepdog when there are no more shepherds.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks what happens to a working sheepdog when there are no more shepherds.
portrait: Nora is the **stock manager** on Glebe House Farm, loyal to the Whitlocks after twenty-three years.
She has **never used AI** and trusts her dogs and notebook over any screen.
Her husband Daniel's **tanker job** makes the household exposed from Steady Disruption onwards.
In fast AGI she is **alarmed** at losing both incomes in the same year.
With time she'd buy **a few acres** and a flock, so no machine or boss can say she's not needed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both her job and Daniel's gone in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: Making firms **keep people on longer** so job losses aren't all at once.
Help for families to **buy land**, not handouts.
